spec.focus: Ideas about war, peace and the power of states in Europe in the late eighteenth century (the document is a philosopher's proposal, not a description of events; part A must ask only about what the excerpt says about standing armies and why; parts B and C ask about well-known European events and arrangements between 1789 and 1815, and any comparison with the excerpt must be about standing armies and the risk of war only, because the excerpt contains nothing else)

sources.context: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher who taught at the University of Konigsberg in Prussia; he published this essay in 1795.

payload.title: Kant on Standing Armies and the Wars of 1789 to 1815

prompt.scenario: In the late eighteenth century, European philosophers debated whether war between states could be limited or ended. In 1795, while Europe was at war with revolutionary France, the Prussian philosopher Immanuel Kant published a proposal for a lasting peace among states. Between 1789 and 1815, European states fought a long series of wars and then negotiated a new peace settlement.
requirements: Each part requires one specific, accurate response.
Part A must be based on what the excerpt itself says.
Parts B and C must use specific historical evidence from the period 1789 to 1815 beyond the excerpt.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE reason Kant gives in the excerpt for abolishing standing armies.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific military development or event in Europe in the period 1789 to 1815 that either supports or challenges Kant's argument that standing armies increase the risk of war.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way the peace arrangements made by the European great powers in 1814 to 1815 either resembled or differed from Kant's proposal about standing armies and the risk of war.

sources.title: Perpetual Peace, first preliminary article 3 (excerpt on standing armies)

sources.context: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher who taught at the University of Konigsberg in Prussia; he published this essay in 1795.
sources.body: Standing armies (miles perpetuus) shall be abolished in course of time.” For they are always threatening other states with war by appearing to be in constant readiness to fight. They incite the various states to outrival one another in the number of their soldiers, and to this number no limit can be set. Now, since owing to the sums devoted to this purpose, peace at last becomes even more oppressive than a short war, these standing armies are themselves the cause of wars of aggression, undertaken in order to get rid of this burden. To which we must add that the practice of hiring men to kill or to be killed seems to imply a use of them as mere machines and instruments in the hand of another (namely, the state) which cannot easily be reconciled with the right of humanity in our own person.

rows.name: Part A

descriptors.0: The response gives no reason, gives a reason the excerpt does not contain, or only repeats that Kant wanted armies abolished.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one reason the excerpt gives for abolishing standing armies.

rows.task_specific: Students describe one reason the excerpt gives for abolishing standing armies: their constant readiness threatens other states; they push states into competing over troop numbers with no limit; their cost makes peace more burdensome than a short war and so leads to wars of aggression; or paying men to kill or be killed treats them as tools of the state, which conflicts with the right of humanity.

rows.name: Part B

descriptors.0: The response names no specific development, gives one outside 1789 to 1815, or does not link it to standing armies and the risk of war.
descriptors.1: The response explains one specific, accurate development from 1789 to 1815 and how it supports or challenges Kant's argument about standing armies and war.

rows.task_specific: Students explain one specific European military development or event from 1789 to 1815, such as the levee en masse of 1793, French conscription laws, the growth of Napoleon's armies, the Prussian military reforms after 1806, or the 1812 invasion of Russia, and connect it to Kant's claim that standing armies raise the risk of war. Students may argue that it supports or challenges the claim.

rows.name: Part C

descriptors.0: The response does not identify an accurate feature of the 1814 to 1815 arrangements, or it compares them with Kant on something other than standing armies or the risk of war.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate similarity or difference between the 1814 to 1815 arrangements and Kant's proposal about standing armies and the risk of war.

rows.task_specific: Students explain one similarity or difference between the 1814 to 1815 peace arrangements (the Congress of Vienna, the Treaties of Paris, the Quadruple Alliance, the Holy Alliance, the Concert of Europe) and Kant's proposal. The comparison must be about standing armies or the risk of war. The most likely difference is that the powers kept large standing armies and relied on a balance of power and joint military commitments rather than disarmament. A likely similarity is that the powers shared Kant's goal of preventing future wars of aggression.

scoring_notes: Part A must rest on the excerpt itself. Do not credit claims about Kant's other preliminary or definitive articles, such as republican constitutions or a federation of states, because the excerpt does not contain them.

In Part B, credit both supporting and challenging answers. For example, a student may argue that mass conscription shows armies growing with no limit, which supports Kant, or that the citizen army of 1793 was raised to defend the revolution rather than for a planned war of aggression, which complicates his argument.
In Part C, do not credit a description of the Vienna settlement alone. The response must connect it to standing armies or to preventing war.
Do not penalize minor errors in dates or spelling if the development is clearly identified and accurately described.

contextualization_ideas: Eighteenth-century dynastic states kept permanent professional armies, and Frederick the Great's Prussia was a well-known example.
Enlightenment thinkers applied reason to questions of international order and human dignity.
Kant published the essay in 1795, while the wars between revolutionary France and the European monarchies were under way, and in the same year as the Peace of Basel.
outside_evidence: Napoleon's Grande Armee and the 1812 Russian campaign
Congress of Vienna and the balance of power
Quadruple Alliance and the Concert of Europe
Second Treaty of Paris (1815) and the allied occupation of France
reasoning_types: Sourcing and claims: identifying an argument in a primary source
Causation: connecting military growth to the risk of war
Comparison: contrasting Kant's proposal with the 1815 settlement

doc_uses.source_id: Kant, Perpetual Peace (1795), first preliminary article 3
doc_uses.usable_for: Identifying Enlightenment arguments against standing armies: the threat they pose, arms competition, financial burden, and the moral objection to using soldiers as instruments.
doc_uses.sourcing: This is a normative philosophical proposal by a Prussian university philosopher, published in 1795 during the wars with revolutionary France. It sets out what states should do and does not describe events.

a: Kant says standing armies always threaten other states with war because they appear to be in constant readiness to fight.
Kant argues that standing armies push states to outdo one another in the number of their soldiers, and that this competition has no natural limit.
Kant claims that the cost of maintaining standing armies makes peace more oppressive than a short war, so states start wars of aggression to get rid of the burden.
Kant objects that hiring men to kill or be killed uses them as mere machines or instruments of the state, which conflicts with the right of humanity in each person.
b: The French levee en masse of 1793 called the whole nation to serve the war effort and produced armies much larger than earlier ones. This supports Kant's point that the number of soldiers can grow without limit and pull states into wider war.

Napoleon's large conscript armies, such as the multinational force he led into Russia in 1812, show military power being used for wars of conquest across Europe. This supports Kant's claim that large standing forces encourage aggression.

After its defeat by Napoleon in 1806, Prussia was forced to limit the size of its army, and reformers such as Scharnhorst and Gneisenau rebuilt it. The other powers answered France by enlarging and reorganizing their own armies, which matches the competition over troop numbers that Kant describes.

Revolutionary France's war against Austria and Prussia, which began in 1792, was driven largely by ideological fears and political conflict, not only by the burden of keeping standing armies. This complicates Kant's claim that standing armies are themselves the cause of wars of aggression.
c: The Vienna settlement differed from Kant's proposal because the great powers did not abolish standing armies. Austria, Prussia, Russia and Britain kept large military forces and relied on a balance of power to deter aggression.

The Quadruple Alliance of November 1815 committed Austria, Prussia, Russia and Britain to act together, including by force, against a renewed French threat. This differed from Kant because it used combined military power, not disarmament, to keep the peace.

Under the Second Treaty of Paris of 1815, allied troops occupied part of France for a period of years. This differed from Kant because peace was enforced with standing armies rather than by removing them.

The peacemakers resembled Kant in one goal: like him, they wanted to keep any single state from launching wars of aggression. They pursued this through great-power consultation in the Concert of Europe instead of abolishing armies.

common_pitfalls: Attributing to the excerpt ideas from other parts of Perpetual Peace, such as republican government or a league of nations, which the excerpt does not contain.
Saying that Kant described or reported on actual events. The excerpt is a philosophical proposal, not an account of events.
In Part B, naming a war or battle without explaining how it relates to standing armies or the risk of war.
In Part C, describing the Congress of Vienna's territorial changes without relating them to armies or war prevention.
Claiming that the Congress of Vienna disarmed Europe or abolished standing armies, which is inaccurate.
Using developments from after 1815, or from the United States, as main evidence.
facts: Immanuel Kant taught at the University of Konigsberg in Prussia and published Perpetual Peace in 1795.
In 1795 Prussia made a separate peace with France, the Peace of Basel, and left the war against France.
France declared war on Austria in April 1792, beginning the French Revolutionary Wars; Prussia joined Austria.
The National Convention decreed the levee en masse in August 1793.
The Jourdan Law of 1798 established regular conscription in France.
Napoleon defeated Prussia at Jena and Auerstedt in 1806, and the Treaties of Tilsit followed in 1807.
Prussian military reform after 1806 was associated with Scharnhorst and Gneisenau.
Napoleon invaded Russia in 1812 with a very large multinational army.
The Congress of Vienna met in 1814 to 1815.
The Holy Alliance (Russia, Austria and Prussia) and the Quadruple Alliance (Austria, Prussia, Russia and Britain) were formed in 1815.
The Second Treaty of Paris (1815) included an allied occupation of part of France and an indemnity.

spec.focus: The division of Berlin and the confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union in 1961 (the sign in the photograph is not readable; make no claims about its words or about which side of any boundary the people stand on; part A may ask only about objects and actions that are clearly visible, such as the tank, its crew in the hatches, the uniformed men and the barrier)

payload.title: A U.S. Tank at Checkpoint Charlie, Berlin, 1961

prompt.scenario: In the period c. 1945 to 1990, Berlin was a focal point of the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union, and in 1961 the city's division became a scene of open military confrontation.
requirements: Each part requires one specific, historically accurate response.
Part A must rest on what can actually be seen in the photograph.
Parts B and C must use specific developments from the years named in each part.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE visible feature of the photograph that shows military power being displayed at the Berlin crossing point in 1961.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development in the period 1945 to 1961, not shown in the photograph, that helps explain why United States military forces faced Soviet-bloc forces in Berlin in 1961.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development in the period 1962 to 1990 that changed or ended the division of Berlin and Germany.

rows.task_specific: Describes one clearly visible element of the photograph that shows military power at the crossing point, such as the U.S. Army tank with its white star and front blade, the crew in the hatches, the long gun barrel, or the uniformed men standing near the barrier gate.

rows.name: Part B

descriptors.0: The response gives no development, a development outside 1945 to 1961, an inaccurate one, or only restates the photograph.
descriptors.1: The response explains how one specific, accurate development from 1945 to 1961 helps account for U.S. and Soviet-bloc forces confronting each other in Berlin in 1961.

rows.task_specific: Explains one specific development from 1945 to 1961 that accounts for the U.S.-Soviet confrontation in Berlin, such as the four-power occupation agreed by the wartime Allies, the Berlin Blockade and Airlift of 1948-1949, the founding of two German states in 1949, the large flow of East Germans to the West through Berlin, Khrushchev's 1958 demand that the Western powers leave Berlin, or the construction of the Berlin Wall beginning in August 1961.

rows.name: Part C

descriptors.0: The response gives no development, one outside 1962 to 1990, an inaccurate one, or does not connect it to the division of Berlin or Germany.
descriptors.1: The response explains how one specific, accurate development from 1962 to 1990 changed or ended the division of Berlin and Germany.

rows.task_specific: Explains one specific development from 1962 to 1990 that changed or ended the division, such as Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik and the 1972 Basic Treaty, the 1975 Helsinki Accords, Gorbachev's reforms and his move away from using force in Eastern Europe, Hungary's opening of its border with Austria in 1989, the opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989, or German reunification on 3 October 1990.

scoring_notes: Each part is scored on its own; a response can earn 0 to 3 points.
In part A, do not reward claims about the words on the sign or about which side of the boundary any person stands on, because the photograph does not show these clearly.

Do not reward a part B response that only says Berlin was split into sectors, since the context line already gives that information. A response that explains the four-power occupation agreement as the reason Western troops were in the city may earn the point.

A response does not need to date the photograph to a specific month; the October 1961 tank standoff at Checkpoint Charlie may be used as context but should not be claimed as the moment the picture was taken.

contextualization_ideas: The postwar occupation of Germany and the growing split between the wartime Allies.
Berlin as an island of Western control inside the Soviet zone and then inside the GDR.
outside_evidence: Kennedy's 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech, June 1963

doc_uses.usable_for: Evidence of armed U.S. presence and a guarded crossing point in divided Berlin in 1961.
doc_uses.sourcing: A U.S. Army photograph taken from above. Because the Army made it, it may have been meant to record or show American resolve, but the credit line does not say what it was for.

a: A large U.S. Army tank marked with a white star is parked across the street at the crossing, a show of armed American strength.
Crew members can be seen in the tank's hatches, which suggests the tank was manned and ready rather than parked and empty.
The tank's long gun barrel points along the street at the crossing, showing that heavy weapons had been brought right up to the checkpoint.
Several uniformed men stand near a barrier gate beyond the tank, showing that the crossing was controlled and guarded.
b: The Berlin Blockade of 1948-1949 and the Western airlift showed that the United States would commit itself to keeping West Berlin, which helps explain why U.S. forces were still there and ready to stand firm in 1961.

Large numbers of East Germans left for the West through Berlin in the 1950s, which led East German and Soviet leaders to seal the border with the Berlin Wall in August 1961 and raised tensions with the Western powers.
In 1958 Khrushchev demanded that the Western powers leave Berlin and that it become a free city, which began a long crisis that was still unresolved in 1961.
The creation of two rival German states in 1949, tied to NATO and later the Warsaw Pact, made Berlin the place where the two blocs touched directly.
c: Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik, including the 1972 Basic Treaty between the two German states, eased the division by setting up formal relations and making contacts and travel easier.
Gorbachev's reforms and his choice not to use Soviet force to keep the East European regimes in power allowed the East German regime to collapse in 1989.
Hungary's opening of its border with Austria in 1989 let thousands of East Germans escape west, which added pressure leading to the opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989.
German reunification on 3 October 1990 ended the division of Germany and of Berlin.

common_pitfalls: Claiming to read the sign or saying which side of the boundary particular figures stand on.
Saying that the photograph definitely shows the October 1961 tank standoff.
In part B, only restating that Berlin had an American sector and an eastern sector, which is already in the context line.
In part C, picking events outside 1962-1990 or events that did not affect the German division, such as only naming the Cuban Missile Crisis without linking it to Berlin.
Confusing the Berlin Blockade (1948-1949) with the building of the Wall (1961).
facts: After 1945 the four occupying powers (United States, Britain, France, Soviet Union) divided Berlin into sectors, though the city lay inside the Soviet zone of Germany.
The Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin's land routes in 1948-1949, and the Western powers supplied the city by airlift.
The Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic were both founded in 1949.
Construction of the Berlin Wall began on 13 August 1961.
In October 1961, U.S. and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie.
The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989, and Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.
